title: Structural Typing, satisfies & Index Signatures
description: How TypeScript decides type compatibility, excess property checks, index signatures, and the satisfies operator.

challenges.title: Structural vs nominal typing
challenges.whyMatters: Structural typing is the single most important thing to understand about TypeScript's type system. It determines when types are compatible, which shapes every design decision you make.
hints: TypeScript checks shape, not name — if it has the right properties, it's compatible

choices.label: Compile error — Point and Coordinate are different named types
Works — TypeScript is structurally typed. Coordinate has the same shape as Point so it is compatible, regardless of the name
Works only because both are interfaces, not classes
Works at runtime but TypeScript shows a warning

challenges.title: Excess property checks
challenges.whyMatters: Excess property checks only fire on fresh object literals — understanding this prevents confusion when passing variables works but inline literals don't.
hints: Excess property checks only apply to object literals assigned directly to a typed variable — not through an intermediate variable

choices.label: Both fail — extra properties are never allowed
Both pass — extra properties are always fine structurally
Case A fails (excess property check on fresh literal) · Case B passes (variable assignment uses structural compatibility, no freshness check)
Case A passes · Case B fails

challenges.title: Write types that demonstrate structural compatibility
challenges.description:
Demonstrate structural typing rules:

1. Write `isCompatible<T>(value: unknown, check: (v: unknown) => v is T): value is T` — a generic structural check wrapper

2. Write three interfaces:
   - `Animal` with `name: string` and `sound(): string`
   - `Pet` with `name: string`, `sound(): string`, and `owner: string`
   - `Named` with just `name: string`

3. Write `greet(a: Named): string` — returns `'Hello, {name}!'`

4. Write `makeSound(a: Animal): string` — returns `'{name} says {sound()}'`

Demonstrate by creating a `Pet` object and passing it to both functions — show that structural compatibility allows this without explicit casting.
challenges.whyMatters: Structural typing enables duck-typed interfaces — your service client, your test double, and your mock all satisfy the same interface without declaring it.
hints: Pet is structurally compatible with both Animal and Named — it has all their properties and more
No casting needed — TypeScript sees the shape automatically
isCompatible: call check(value) and return the result

challenges.title: Index signatures
challenges.whyMatters: Index signature constraints trip up everyone the first time. Knowing the rule — all named properties must be assignable to the index signature's value type — prevents mysterious errors when mixing typed and dynamic properties.
hints: When you have [key: string]: string, every property including named ones must be string

choices.label: No error — named properties are exempt from the index signature constraint
Error: 'count' of type 'number' is not assignable to string index type 'string' — all named properties must match the index signature value type
Error: you cannot combine an index signature with named properties
No error at declaration, but error when you access .count

challenges.title: Write types with index signatures
challenges.description:
Write these index signature patterns:

1. `interface MetricsMap` — string keys, number values, PLUS a required named `timestamp: number` property. Fix the conflict so both work.

2. `interface FlexibleConfig` — string keys mapping to `string | number | boolean`, with named required fields `name: string` and `version: number`

3. Write `mergeConfigs(base: FlexibleConfig, overrides: Partial<FlexibleConfig>): FlexibleConfig` — merges override into base, returning new object

4. Write `getMetric(map: MetricsMap, key: string): number | undefined` — safely reads a value, returns undefined for missing keys
challenges.whyMatters: Mixed index + named property interfaces are common in config objects and metric maps — things that have known required fields but also accept arbitrary extra data.
hints: To fix the MetricsMap conflict: make the index value string | number, then timestamp: number is compatible
FlexibleConfig: [key: string]: string | number | boolean — name and version are both assignable to that union
mergeConfigs: return { ...base, ...overrides } (spreading Partial is fine — undefined values don't overwrite)

challenges.title: The satisfies operator
challenges.whyMatters: satisfies validates a value against a type without losing the literal or narrow type. Used for typed config objects where you want both validation AND autocomplete on specific keys.
hints: satisfies checks the shape but keeps the inferred type — annotation widens to the declared type

choices.label: colors2.red is string — same as annotation
colors2.red is '#ff0000' — satisfies validates the shape but preserves the literal type inference
colors2.red is string | undefined — satisfies adds undefined safety
Compile error — satisfies cannot be used with Record types

challenges.title: Use satisfies for typed config
challenges.description:
Use `satisfies` to build validated configs that preserve narrow types:

1. Define `RouteConfig` with index signature: `{ [path: string]: { method: 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE'; handler: string } }`

2. Create `routes` using `satisfies RouteConfig` — include at least `/health`, `/api/users`, `/api/users/:id`. Each with appropriate methods and handler names.

3. Write `getHandler(routes: RouteConfig, path: string): string | undefined`

4. Write `listRoutes(routes: RouteConfig): string[]` — returns `['GET /health', 'POST /api/users', ...]`

The key: with `satisfies`, accessing `routes['/health'].method` should give you the literal type (e.g. `'GET'`), not just `'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE'`.
challenges.whyMatters: Route config tables defined with satisfies give you autocomplete on known routes and type-checked methods — without losing the flexibility of a dynamic record.
hints: const routes = { '/health': { method: 'GET', handler: 'healthHandler' }, ... } satisfies RouteConfig

challenges.title: Type compatibility in practice
challenges.description:
Write a function compatibility demonstration:

1. `type Logger = { log(msg: string): void }`
   `type DetailedLogger = { log(msg: string, level: string): void }`

   Write `acceptsLogger(l: Logger): void` and show which of these is assignable to Logger:
   - `{ log(msg: string): void }` — basic
   - `{ log(msg: string, level?: string): void }` — optional extra param  
   - `{ log(msg: string, level: string): void }` — required extra param
   - `{ log(msg: string): void; warn(msg: string): void }` — extra method

2. Write a `compose<T, U, V>(f: (x: T) => U, g: (x: U) => V): (x: T) => V` and show structural typing making it work with compatible (not identical) function types.

3. Export a `results` object documenting which assignments are valid with comments explaining why.
challenges.whyMatters: Function parameter compatibility — especially the optional param rule — is a common source of TypeScript confusion. Understanding it means you stop fighting the compiler and start working with it.
hints: Functions with fewer required params are assignable to function types with more — not the reverse
Extra optional params: assignable. Extra required params: not assignable.
Extra methods on an object: always fine (structural supertype is assignable to subtype)
